script: Artificial intelligence is no longer a concept of the future. It is the defining force of our present. From the moment you wake up and check your phone, to the algorithms that power global financial markets — AI is already woven into the fabric of daily life. But how did we get here? And more importantly, where are we going? In the 1950s, a British mathematician named Alan Turing posed a deceptively simple question: Can machines think? That single question ignited decades of research, failure, and breakthrough. Early AI systems were rigid — they could only do what they were explicitly programmed to do. Then came machine learning. Instead of programming rules, scientists began feeding machines data and letting them find the patterns themselves. The results were startling. Machines began recognizing faces, translating languages, and beating world champions at chess. Today, large language models like GPT and Claude can write poetry, debug code, and hold nuanced conversations. They are trained on hundreds of billions of words — the collected knowledge of human civilization. But with this power comes profound responsibility. Questions of bias, privacy, job displacement, and existential risk are no longer science fiction. They are board room conversations. The nations and companies that lead in AI will shape the economic and political landscape of the 21st century. This is not merely a technological revolution. It is a civilizational one.
